title: Ebay Has to Pay $55.7 Million in Settlement for Its Unhinged Harassment Campaign
gist: eBay and three former executives settled the Steiner harassment civil suit for $55.7 million total, with $46.15 million from the company and personal payments from ex-CEO Devin Wenig and two other executives. The settlement carries no confidentiality clause and rests on a novel argument that eBay's California domicile allowed punitive damages otherwise barred in Massachusetts — a precedent for cross-state harassment claims.

themes.theme: Settlement economics and personal executive liability

insights.claim: The civil settlement pays David and Ina Steiner more than $46.15 million from eBay plus $2 million from former CEO Devin Wenig, $500,000 from former executive Wendy Jones and $50,000 from former executive Steve Wymer.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Named executives paying personally out of a corporate harassment case raises the expected cost of D&O coverage and changes the risk calculus for aggressive comms tactics.
insights.locator: The Steiners will receive more than $46.15 million

insights.claim: On top of the individual payouts, eBay is giving $6 million to charity and Wenig an additional $1 million to a nonprofit that protects First Amendment rights, and the company must issue a strongly worded statement condemning the former employees.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Non-cash remedies like compelled public statements are becoming part of settlement design, extending reputational cost beyond the dollar figure.
insights.locator: EBay is also giving $6 million to charity

insights.claim: The civil settlement dwarfs the $3 million criminal penalty eBay had earlier agreed to pay the US Attorney's Office in the District of Massachusetts, roughly a fifteen-fold gap between criminal and civil exposure.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Criminal penalties are a poor proxy for total corporate liability; civil follow-on suits are where the real numbers land.
insights.locator: EBay later agreed to pay a $3 million criminal penalty

themes.theme: A new punitive-damages precedent for cross-state harassment

insights.claim: Massachusetts normally bars punitive damages in standard personal injury or civil harassment cases, but the plaintiffs' lawyers successfully argued that because eBay is domiciled in California, where such damages are allowed, they should apply here.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Corporate domicile can import a plaintiff-friendlier damages regime into a hostile forum — a materially expanded liability channel for California-domiciled tech firms.
insights.locator: One subtlety of the Steiner settlement involves a law

insights.claim: Plaintiffs' attorney Chris Murphy believes this is the first time such damages have been allowed in this kind of case in Massachusetts and that it sets a new precedent for harassment campaigns originating from other states.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: If the precedent holds, out-of-state corporate conduct becomes actionable with punitive exposure in states that otherwise disallow it — watch for copycat filings.
insights.locator: Murphy says that he believes it’s the first time

themes.theme: Discovery and the refusal of confidentiality

insights.claim: The settlement contains no confidentiality provision, which the plaintiffs' attorney says was a dealbreaker from day one because the Steiners wanted everyone to see and understand what eBay did to them.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Loss of the confidentiality shield means the reputational tail of a settlement can now outlast the payment — a rising cost of litigating against motivated journalist-plaintiffs.
insights.quote: “From day one, that was a dealbreaker,” says Chris Murphy, an attorney for the Steiners at the personal injury firm Scalli Murphy Law in Everett, Massachusetts.
insights.locator: Notably, the settlement contains no confidentiality provision

insights.claim: Filing the civil suit gave the Steiners access to 68,000 documents they would never have seen through the federal criminal investigation, where as victims they were told very little.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Civil discovery, not prosecution, is the mechanism that surfaces corporate culture evidence — a structural reason companies should fear the civil track more.
insights.quote: “We were often in the dark during the federal investigation, and we were told very little as victims,” she said.
insights.locator: Ina Steiner underscored that the couple ultimately pursued

insights.claim: David Steiner frames the outcome as only partial resolution, saying it will take a while to see what a settlement means in the bigger context versus having gone to trial.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Settlements avoid a jury verdict but leave the deterrence question open — the precedent value is legal, not adjudicated fact.
insights.quote: “It’s a relief in some sense that we have some finality,”

insights.claim: The campaign against the Steiners ran over roughly two months in the summer of 2019, escalating from anonymous threatening Twitter DMs to home deliveries including a bloody pig mask, pornography, fly larvae, live spiders and live cockroaches.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: The specificity of the conduct is why the damages number is an outlier; it is not a template for ordinary reputational disputes.
insights.locator: According to the initial criminal complaints

insights.claim: The campaign extended to in-person surveillance in a rented Dodge Caravan and to Craigslist classified ads for a swinger party, a threesome, a block sale and an estate sale, all pointing strangers to the Steiners' home address.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Weaponizing third-party platforms as harassment infrastructure is the operational detail that turned a comms dispute into criminal conduct.
insights.locator: Eventually, the eBay workers turned to in-person surveillance

insights.claim: The harassers eased up and scrambled to cover their tracks only once the couple alerted the Natick police department, who in turn alerted federal authorities.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Escalation stopped at law-enforcement contact, not at internal controls — evidence that no corporate guardrail caught it.
insights.locator: Once the couple alerted the Natick police department

insights.claim: Six former eBay employees and one contractor were charged in 2020, and the couple filed their civil suit in 2021, meaning the matter took roughly seven years from conduct to final civil settlement.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Multi-year tail risk: conduct from 2019 was still generating new headline liability in 2026.
insights.locator: Back in 2020, six former eBay employees

themes.theme: Command responsibility and the corporate defense

insights.claim: Devin Wenig allegedly gave the initial order to 'take her down' regarding Ina Steiner to chief communications officer Steve Wymer, though his lawyers maintain and court documents appear to support that he meant a communications plan.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Ambiguous executive language cascading into criminal conduct is the core governance failure mode here — and it still cost Wenig $3 million personally.
insights.locator: While Wenig has maintained that he had no knowledge

insights.claim: eBay's public response leans on discontinuity, extending its deepest apologies while emphasizing that new leadership is in charge and that the 2019 incidents are not representative of the company's culture today.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: The standard 'different management now' defense; investors should test whether governance changes are structural or rhetorical.

insights.claim: eBay's statement acknowledged 'the unprofessional tone in internal communications' demonstrated to different degrees by Wenig, Wymer and Jones, an admission that the problem reached beyond the seven charged individuals.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Company-acknowledged executive-level tone problems are a discoverable governance red flag in future litigation.

insights.claim: The Steiners remained in their Natick home throughout the harassment and the pandemic, enhancing home security and sleeping in separate rooms in case one was physically assaulted at night.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: Illustrates why damages were assessed high — sustained fear of physical harm, not mere reputational injury.
insights.locator: Murphy made a point to say that they remained

insights.claim: EcommerceBytes is still operating, and Ina Steiner broke the settlement news on her own site just after 9 pm local time, ahead of every other outlet.
insights.speaker: Lauren Goode
insights.so_what: The targeted publication survived the campaign intact — the attempted suppression failed on its own terms.
insights.locator: Ina Steiner’s most recent post, about the settlement
